steps.p: The front door of the cluster. Every kubectl command, every controller, every kubelet talks to it over HTTPS. It validates requests, applies RBAC, and writes state to etcd.
The key-value store holding the entire cluster state. If etcd is lost and not backed up, the cluster is gone. It runs on port 2379 and only the apiserver should talk to it.
The scheduler assigns pods to nodes based on resources, affinity and taints. The controller-manager runs reconciliation loops: deployment, replicaset, node, endpoints.

ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd.db --write-out=table shows revision, total keys and size. Always verify a snapshot before you need it.
etcdctl snapshot restore /backup/etcd.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore, then point the etcd static pod hostPath to the new data dir and restart it.
A Role is namespaced. A ClusterRole is cluster-wide and is needed for nodes, persistentvolumes and namespaces themselves.
kubectl create rolebinding dev --role=pod-reader --user=jane -n dev. Without a binding, a Role grants nothing.
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=jane -n dev answers yes or no. It is the fastest way to prove a permission in the exam.
apt-get install kubeadm=1.x.y, then kubeadm upgrade plan, then kubeadm upgrade apply v1.x.y. Drain the node first if it is also a worker.
On each worker: drain, install the new kubeadm and kubelet, kubeadm upgrade node, restart kubelet, uncordon.
Upgrade the control plane before any worker, and never skip a minor version: 1.28 to 1.30 goes through 1.29.
A CRD adds a new kind to the API. Once applied, kubectl get <kind> works and the object is stored in etcd like any other resource.
An operator is a controller watching a custom resource and reconciling real infrastructure: databases, certs, backups. Install it with its CRDs, in the right order.
You are usually asked to install an operator from a manifest and create one custom resource. Read the CRD to know the required fields.
clusters, users and contexts, plus current-context. A context is the pair user + cluster + namespace.
kubectl config use-context cka. kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=dev changes only the namespace.
Every task starts by checking the context and namespace. Solving a task in the wrong namespace scores zero.
Container runtime (containerd), swap disabled, br_netfilter and ip_forward sysctls, kubelet kubeadm kubectl installed and pinned.
kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16, then copy /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf to ~/.kube/config and install the CNI.
kubeadm token create --print-join-command on the control plane, run it on each worker. Remove the control-plane taint to schedule there.

lessons.t: Using the docs during the exam

steps.p: kubernetes.io/docs, kubernetes.io/blog and helm.sh/docs, in one extra tab. No forum, no blog, no AI assistant.
kubectl cheat sheet, NetworkPolicy, PV, probes, taints, RBAC. Finding a page in 30 seconds instead of 5 minutes is the difference between finishing and not.
The docs contain complete manifests. Copy, paste, adapt the names. Do not retype a NetworkPolicy from memory.
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=3, then kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5.
kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:1.27 triggers a rolling update. kubectl rollout status deployment/web follows it.
kubectl rollout history deployment/web shows revisions; kubectl rollout undo deployment/web --to-revision=1 goes back.
kubectl create configmap app --from-literal=COLOR=blue --from-file=app.conf. Consume it as env vars or as a volume.
kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=password=s3cr3t. Values are base64 encoded, not encrypted, unless encryption at rest is configured.
volumes: [{name: cfg, configMap: {name: app}}] then volumeMounts in the container. Updating the ConfigMap updates the file, not the env var.
requests decide where a pod can be scheduled; limits decide what it may consume. A pod without requests is Burstable and can be evicted first.
nodeSelector is a simple label match. nodeAffinity adds operators and required/preferred rules for more complex placement.
kubectl taint nodes node1 key=value:NoSchedule repels pods. Only pods with the matching toleration can land there. It does not force them to.
livenessProbe restarts a stuck container. A wrong liveness probe causes CrashLoopBackOff, a classic exam trap.
readinessProbe removes the pod from Service endpoints until it passes. Use it for slow starts.
startupProbe gives a slow application time to boot before liveness and readiness begin.
Runs pods until a number of successful completions. backoffLimit caps retries, completions and parallelism control the shape.
schedule uses five fields, in UTC. concurrencyPolicy Forbid prevents overlapping runs, successfulJobsHistoryLimit cleans up.
A CronJob that never runs is often a wrong schedule field count or a suspended: true flag.
Run one after another before the app starts, each must succeed. Typical use: wait for a database, clone a repo, fix permissions.
A second container in the same pod sharing network and volumes: log shipper, proxy, metrics exporter.
kubectl logs pod -c init-container shows why the init phase is stuck. A CrashLooping init container blocks the whole pod.
The HPA needs metrics-server and resource requests on the pods. Without requests, the CPU percentage is unknown and the HPA does nothing.
kubectl autoscale deployment web --cpu-percent=70 --min=2 --max=10.
kubectl get hpa shows TARGETS as <unknown>/70% when metrics are missing. Fix metrics-server before blaming the HPA.
Default type, reachable only inside the cluster. It load balances across pods matching its selector.
Opens a port on every node between 30000 and 32767. Useful for quick access, not for production.
Asks the cloud provider for an external load balancer. On bare metal it stays pending unless something like MetalLB is installed.
A NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {} and policyTypes: [Ingress] blocks all inbound traffic in that namespace. Nothing is denied until a policy selects the pod.
Combine podSelector, ingress.from.podSelector and namespaceSelector to allow only chosen sources, on chosen ports.
Add policyTypes: [Egress] and egress.to rules. Without an egress rule, selected pods cannot reach DNS either.
An Ingress object does nothing without an ingress controller (nginx, traefik). Install the controller first.
ingress.spec.rules[].host plus paths with pathType Prefix route traffic to a Service name and port.
Reference a kubernetes.io/tls Secret in spec.tls to terminate HTTPS at the controller.
Every Service gets <name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. Short names work inside the same namespace.
Run kubectl run tmp --image=busybox --rm -it -- nslookup kubernetes.default. If it fails, check CoreDNS pods in kube-system.
clusterIP: None returns pod IPs directly instead of a virtual IP, used by StatefulSets.
Every pod gets its own IP, routable inside the cluster without NAT. The CNI plugin implements this: Calico, Cilium, Flannel, Weave.
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|flannel'. No CNI means pods stay in ContainerCreating or nodes stay NotReady.
Only some CNIs enforce policies. Calico and Cilium do; plain Flannel does not. That explains a policy that seems ignored.
ClusterIP is virtual: kube-proxy programs iptables or IPVS. There is no process listening on that IP.
clusterIP: None returns the pod IPs directly through DNS, used by StatefulSets and clients that need per-pod addressing.
Returns a CNAME to an external DNS name, no proxying, no endpoints. Useful to point a Service at a managed database.
kubectl create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key creates the kubernetes.io/tls secret the Ingress expects.
spec.tls[].hosts must match spec.rules[].host, and the secretName must exist in the same namespace as the Ingress.
kubectl describe ingress shows the controller events. A default backend 404 usually means a path or host mismatch.
<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local resolves to the ClusterIP. Short name works inside the same namespace only.
<pod-ip-with-hyphens>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local resolves directly to a pod, even without a Service.
nslookup from a busybox pod. If the name fails but the IP works, it is DNS, not networking.
A PersistentVolume is cluster storage: capacity, accessModes and a backend such as hostPath, NFS or a cloud disk.
A PersistentVolumeClaim asks for size and access mode. Kubernetes binds it to a matching PV. A Pending PVC almost always means no matching PV.
ReadWriteOnce is one node, ReadOnlyMany many nodes read-only, ReadWriteMany many nodes writable (not supported by every backend).
A StorageClass with a provisioner creates PVs on demand when a PVC references it, so you never write PV manifests.
The annotation storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class=true makes it used when a PVC does not specify one.
Delete removes the volume with the PVC, Retain keeps the data. Check it before deleting anything in the exam.
Created with the pod, deleted with it. Shared between containers of the same pod.
Mounts a node directory. Ties the pod to one node and is a security risk, but appears in exam tasks for static pods.
Combines several sources (secret, configMap, serviceAccountToken) into one directory.
A Container Storage Interface driver lets Kubernetes talk to any storage backend. It runs as a DaemonSet plus a controller.
provisioner names the CSI driver, parameters configure it, volumeBindingMode WaitForFirstConsumer delays binding until a pod is scheduled.
WaitForFirstConsumer leaves the PVC Pending until a pod uses it. That is normal, not a failure.
The scheduler cannot place the pod: not enough CPU or memory, unsatisfied nodeSelector, or a taint with no toleration. kubectl describe pod shows the reason in Events.
The image name is wrong, the tag does not exist, or the registry needs a pull secret. Check with kubectl describe pod and the Events section.
The container starts and exits repeatedly. kubectl logs pod --previous shows the last crashed run. A failing liveness probe causes the same state.
Check the kubelet: systemctl status kubelet, journalctl -u kubelet -n 50. Common causes are a stopped kubelet, wrong certificates or a full disk.
Evicted pods mean the node is out of disk or memory. kubectl describe node shows the pressure conditions and the evicted pods.
kubeadm certs check-expiration lists control plane certificates. An expired apiserver certificate breaks every kubectl call.
kubectl get endpoints <svc>. Empty endpoints mean the Service selector does not match any pod label.
targetPort must match the container port, port is the Service port. A mismatch gives connection refused or a timeout.
Test with a temporary pod: kubectl run tmp --image=busybox --rm -it -- wget -qO- http://svc:80. It separates network issues from application issues.
kubectl logs pod, kubectl logs pod -c container for multi-container pods, --previous for the crashed instance.
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -A shows the cluster timeline. It is the first thing to read when something will not start.
kubectl exec -it pod -- sh gives a shell inside the container to test DNS, files and environment variables.
kube-apiserver, etcd, scheduler and controller-manager are static pods. Check crictl ps -a on the control plane node and the manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests.
crictl logs <container-id> or journalctl -u kubelet. A single wrong flag in a manifest keeps the component down.
A failing etcd makes the apiserver unreachable. Check its data dir, disk space, and the certificates in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd.
kubeadm certs check-expiration lists every control plane certificate with its expiry date.
kubeadm certs renew all, then restart the static pods by moving their manifests out and back, or restart kubelet.
x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid on kubectl calls means the apiserver certificate needs renewal.
/var/log/pods/<namespace>_<pod>_<uid>/<container>/0.log when kubectl logs fails or the container runtime misbehaves.
/var/lib/kubelet holds the kubelet config and pki directory. Certificates used by the kubelet live in /var/lib/kubelet/pki.
/etc/cni/net.d/ lists the CNI configuration files. An empty directory explains why pods never get an IP.
Every task ends with the verification: a pod Running, a PVC Bound, a curl returning a string. Read it first, then work backwards.
If a task resists for five minutes, flag it and move on. One candidate scored 16/75 on the first mock by refusing to skip; the second run reached 53/93.
kubectl get <resource> -o yaml > x.yaml, edit, re-apply. Writing manifests from scratch under time pressure is how typos happen.

arch.q: A copy of etcd is required in the exam. Which sequence is correct?
o: etcdctl snapshot save, then verify with snapshot status
arch.w: snapshot save writes a consistent backup; always verify with snapshot status.

arch.q: Which component assigns pods to nodes?
arch.w: The scheduler decides placement; the kubelet runs the pod on the node it was given.

arch.q: What does a ClusterRoleBinding grant?
arch.w: ClusterRoleBinding binds a ClusterRole across the whole cluster.

arch.q: Where is the cluster state stored?
arch.w: etcd is the single source of truth for cluster state.

arch.q: Which command proves that user jane can list pods in dev?
o: kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=jane -n dev
arch.w: auth can-i impersonates the user and answers yes or no directly.

arch.q: Upgrading a cluster from 1.28 to 1.30 requires:
arch.w: kubeadm supports one minor version at a time: 1.28 to 1.29, then 1.29 to 1.30.

arch.q: What port does etcd listen on by default?
arch.w: 2379 is the etcd client port, 2380 is peer. 6443 is the apiserver.

arch.q: A Pod cannot be scheduled because of a taint. What is the fix?
o: Add a toleration to the pod
Delete the taint from the pod
arch.w: Taints repel pods; only a matching toleration lets the pod land on that node.

arch.q: Which file holds the static pod manifests for the control plane?
arch.w: kubelet watches that directory and runs the control plane as static pods.

arch.q: What does kubeadm upgrade plan do?
o: Shows available versions and component compatibility
arch.w: It reports what can be upgraded and warns about version skew, it changes nothing.

arch.q: Which component watches for node failures and marks nodes NotReady?
arch.w: The node controller applies the NotReady condition when heartbeats stop.

arch.q: A ServiceAccount needs to read pods. What must you create?
o: A Role and a RoleBinding to that ServiceAccount
arch.w: The account gets no rights by itself: a Role plus a RoleBinding grants the permission.

arch.q: What must be installed before kubeadm init on a node?
o: A container runtime, swap disabled, kernel modules loaded
arch.w: containerd, swap off, br_netfilter and ip_forward are the prerequisites.

arch.q: Which command prints the join command for a new worker?
arch.w: It generates a fresh bootstrap token and the full join line.

arch.q: A CRD is applied. What can you do next?
o: Create objects of the new kind with kubectl
arch.w: The apiserver serves the new kind immediately.

arch.q: Which field of a kubeconfig selects the active cluster and user?
arch.w: current-context names the context in use.

arch.q: How do you make the default namespace dev for every command?
arch.w: It edits the current context, so all later commands default to dev.

arch.q: Which certificate file does etcd use for its client connections?
arch.w: client calls use server.crt and server.key with the etcd CA.

arch.q: An operator is installed but its pods crash. First check?
o: Its CRDs are installed and its logs
arch.w: Missing CRDs are the classic operator failure.

arch.q: Which component would you inspect if scheduling stops cluster-wide?
arch.w: It runs as a static pod on the control plane; check its logs with crictl.

arch.q: Where does the kubelet store its own certificates?
arch.w: Kubelet client and server certs live in /var/lib/kubelet/pki.

arch.q: Which docs site is NOT allowed during the CKA?
arch.w: Only the official Kubernetes and Helm documentation are permitted.

arch.q: A candidate scores 16/75 on the first killer.sh mock. Usual cause?
arch.w: Time management: flag and move on, then come back.

arch.q: Which command copies an existing deployment to edit it?
o: kubectl get deploy web -o yaml > web.yaml
arch.w: Export, edit, re-apply. Faster and safer than writing from scratch.

work.q: Which command rolls back a Deployment to revision 2?
work.w: rollout undo with --to-revision is the exact syntax.

work.q: A ConfigMap is updated. Which consumers see the change automatically?
work.w: Mounted files are refreshed by the kubelet; env vars are read once at container start.

work.q: What happens when a container exceeds its memory limit?
work.w: Memory is not compressible: the kernel kills the process, the pod restarts.

work.q: Which field places a pod only on nodes with disk=ssd?
work.w: nodeSelector is a simple label match on the node.

work.q: A pod has no requests or limits. Which QoS class does it get?
work.w: No requests and no limits means BestEffort, evicted first under pressure.

work.q: What does a NoSchedule taint do?
o: Prevents new pods without a toleration
work.w: It repels new pods that lack a toleration; existing pods stay.

work.q: Which probe restarts a container?
work.w: Liveness failure triggers a restart; readiness only removes endpoints.

work.q: A pod stays Pending. What do you check first?
work.w: Pending is a scheduling problem, and describe shows the scheduler's reason.

work.q: How do you scale a Deployment to 5 replicas?
work.w: kubectl scale is the direct command.

work.q: Which object keeps a fixed identity and storage for each replica?
work.w: StatefulSet gives stable names and per-pod PVCs.

work.q: A DaemonSet ensures:
work.w: DaemonSets run one pod on every node, or on the selected nodes.

work.q: Where do you set a container command override?
work.w: command and args live under the container spec.

work.q: Which field limits retries of a failing Job?
work.w: backoffLimit caps retries before the Job is marked failed.

work.q: A CronJob does not run. Most likely cause?
o: Wrong number of fields in schedule
work.w: schedule needs exactly five fields and runs in UTC.

work.q: Init containers run:
work.w: They run one by one before the main containers start.

work.q: An HPA shows TARGETS unknown. Why?
o: metrics-server missing or no resource requests
work.w: Without metrics and requests the CPU percentage cannot be computed.

work.q: Which object runs one pod on every node?
work.w: DaemonSets are used for agents like kube-proxy and CNI.

work.q: What does kubectl rollout pause do?
o: Stops the rollout without deleting pods
work.w: It freezes changes until rollout resume.

work.q: Which strategy recreates all pods at once?
work.w: Recreate terminates everything before starting the new version.

work.q: Where do you set the number of successful Job completions?
work.w: completions is the target number of successful pods.

work.q: Which field suspends a CronJob without deleting it?
work.w: suspend stops new runs while keeping the object and history.

work.q: A Deployment update is stuck. Which command reveals the reason?
work.w: rollout status waits and prints why the new pods are not ready.

work.q: Which object would you use for a one-shot database migration?
work.w: A Job runs to completion; a Deployment would restart it forever.

work.q: What does kubectl set resources do?
o: Updates requests and limits on a workload
work.w: It patches resources for the containers of the workload.

net.q: Which Service type exposes a port on every node?
net.w: NodePort opens a port in the 30000-32767 range on each node.

net.q: A Service has empty endpoints. Most likely cause?
o: The selector does not match pod labels
net.w: Endpoints are built from pods matching the selector. No match, no endpoint.

net.q: What happens with a NetworkPolicy when nothing selects the pod?
net.w: Policies are additive and only apply to selected pods; unselected pods stay open.

net.q: An Ingress object alone does nothing without:
net.w: The controller is what actually routes traffic.

net.q: Which DNS name reaches a Service across namespaces?
net.w: The full form is service.namespace.svc.cluster.local.

net.q: Which field in a Service maps to the container port?
net.w: targetPort is the container's port; port is the Service's own port.

net.q: How to allow only pods labelled role=frontend to reach role=backend?
o: A NetworkPolicy on backend with ingress from podSelector role=frontend
net.w: The policy lives on the destination and selects allowed sources.

net.q: What does clusterIP: None create?
o: A headless service returning pod IPs
net.w: Headless services are used by StatefulSets for direct pod addressing.

net.q: Which command tests DNS from inside the cluster?
net.w: A temporary busybox pod is the standard DNS test.

net.q: kube-proxy is responsible for:
o: implementing Service virtual IPs on each node
net.w: kube-proxy programs iptables or IPVS rules for Service traffic.

net.q: A LoadBalancer Service stays Pending on bare metal because:
o: no cloud provider assigns an external IP
net.w: Without a load balancer implementation the external IP is never assigned.

net.q: Which port does the apiserver serve HTTPS on?
net.w: 6443 is the secure apiserver port.

net.q: Pods stay in ContainerCreating and nodes are NotReady. Likely cause?
net.w: Without a CNI, pod networking never comes up.

net.q: Which CNI does not enforce NetworkPolicy by default?
net.w: Plain Flannel ignores NetworkPolicy objects.

net.q: ExternalName Service returns:
o: a CNAME to an external DNS name
net.w: It is pure DNS redirection with no proxying.

net.q: What does kubectl create secret tls require?
net.w: It builds a kubernetes.io/tls secret from the two files.

net.q: Ingress TLS host must match:
net.w: The certificate is served for the hosts listed in rules and tls.

net.q: Which port range do NodePort Services use?
net.w: That range is the default, configurable on the apiserver.

net.q: A NetworkPolicy with policyTypes Egress and no egress rule:
net.w: An empty egress list denies all outbound traffic, DNS included.

net.q: Which command shows the ClusterIP and ports of a Service?
net.w: get svc -o wide shows ClusterIP, ports and selector.

net.q: Which DNS name reaches a pod directly?
net.w: Pod DNS uses the IP with hyphens under .pod.cluster.local.

net.q: A busybox pod resolves a Service name but curl hangs. Likely cause?
net.w: DNS works, so the problem is at the traffic layer.

net.q: Which port does kube-proxy use to expose NodePort?
net.w: The default NodePort range is 30000 to 32767.

net.q: Which command shows the selector of a Service?
net.w: describe prints Selector, Endpoints and Events.

stor.q: A PVC stays Pending. Most likely reason?
o: No matching PV and no StorageClass
stor.w: Binding needs either a matching PV or a provisioner through a StorageClass.

stor.q: Which access mode allows one node to mount read-write?
stor.w: RWO means a single node, not a single pod.

stor.q: What does a StorageClass provisioner do?
stor.w: Dynamic provisioning creates the PV when a PVC claims it.

stor.q: The reclaim policy Delete means:
o: the PV is removed with the PVC
stor.w: Delete removes the backing volume; Retain keeps it for manual recovery.

stor.q: How do you make a StorageClass the default?
stor.w: That annotation marks the default class.

stor.q: Which volume survives the pod?
stor.w: A PVC points to storage outside the pod lifecycle.

stor.q: emptyDir is deleted when:
o: the pod is removed from the node
stor.w: emptyDir lives as long as the pod on that node.

stor.q: Which is NOT a valid StorageClass provisioner?
stor.w: pod-scheduler is not a provisioner; no-provisioner is used for static PVs.

stor.q: A StatefulSet needs one volume per replica. What is used?
stor.w: volumeClaimTemplates creates a PVC per replica automatically.

stor.q: Which command shows PVs and their claim?
stor.w: get pv lists STATUS and CLAIM columns.

stor.q: hostPath volumes are risky because:
o: they tie the pod to a node and its filesystem
stor.w: hostPath is node-local: no portability, and a security concern.

stor.q: A pod mounts a Secret as a volume. The Secret is updated. What happens?
o: The file updates after a delay
stor.w: The kubelet refreshes projected secret files, usually within a minute.

stor.q: A PVC with WaitForFirstConsumer stays Pending until:
stor.w: Binding is delayed until a pod is scheduled, which is the intended behaviour.

stor.q: Which volume is deleted with the pod?
stor.w: emptyDir lives exactly as long as the pod on that node.

stor.q: A CSI driver usually runs as:
stor.w: Node plugin as DaemonSet, controller as Deployment or StatefulSet.

stor.q: What does volumeBindingMode Immediate do?
o: Binds the PV as soon as the PVC is created
stor.w: Immediate binds early, which can place data on the wrong zone.

stor.q: A pod needs the same file in three containers. Which volume?
stor.w: emptyDir is shared by all containers of the pod.

stor.q: Which field defines the size requested by a PVC?
stor.w: It is resources.requests.storage, same shape as a pod request.

stor.q: Where do you find why a PVC is not bound?
stor.w: The Events section names the missing StorageClass or PV.

stor.q: Projected volumes can combine:
stor.w: Projected volumes merge several sources into one directory.

stor.q: A PVC is Bound but the pod cannot write. Likely cause?
stor.w: ReadWriteOnce on another node, or a readOnly: true mount.

stor.q: Which command shows the reclaim policy of a PV?
stor.w: The RECLAIM POLICY column appears with get pv or describe pv.

stor.q: Where is the hostPath of a static pod defined?
stor.w: Static pods are plain manifests read by the kubelet.

stor.q: What blocks a PVC from binding to a PV?
stor.w: The PV must satisfy accessModes and have at least the requested capacity.

trbl.q: A pod shows CrashLoopBackOff. First command?
trbl.w: --previous shows the logs of the crashed instance.

trbl.q: ImagePullBackOff means:
trbl.w: Wrong name, tag or missing pull secret.

trbl.q: A node is NotReady. What do you check first?
trbl.w: The kubelet is what reports node status to the apiserver.

trbl.q: Which command lists events sorted by time?
trbl.w: Sorting by lastTimestamp gives the real timeline.

trbl.q: A Service returns connection refused. Likely cause?
o: targetPort does not match the container port
trbl.w: A port mismatch is the classic cause of refused connections.

trbl.q: Evicted pods usually mean:
trbl.w: The kubelet evicts pods when the node is under disk or memory pressure.

trbl.q: A liveness probe fails repeatedly. Result?
o: the container restarts in a loop
trbl.w: Liveness failure restarts the container, which often looks like CrashLoopBackOff.

trbl.q: How do you read logs of one container in a multi-container pod?
trbl.w: -c selects the container.

trbl.q: kubectl exec -it pod -- sh is used to:
o: open a shell inside the container
trbl.w: It is the fastest way to test DNS and files from inside.

trbl.q: A Deployment has 0 available replicas. First thing to check?
o: kubectl describe deployment and the pods
trbl.w: Start from the workload: describe shows why pods are not ready.

trbl.q: CoreDNS pods are CrashLooping. What breaks?
o: Service name resolution inside the cluster
trbl.w: Without DNS, services are unreachable by name.

trbl.q: Which command shows the kubelet logs on a node?
trbl.w: The kubelet runs as a systemd service, so journalctl is the tool.

trbl.q: kubectl returns x509 certificate has expired. First action?
trbl.w: kubeadm certs renew all, then restart the static pods.

trbl.q: Which command lists containers on a node without the apiserver?
trbl.w: crictl talks directly to the container runtime socket.

trbl.q: A static pod manifest has a typo. What happens?
o: The component never starts, kubelet retries
trbl.w: kubelet keeps trying and fails silently in kubectl; check the kubelet logs.

trbl.q: etcd is down. What is the visible symptom?
o: kubectl cannot reach the apiserver at all
trbl.w: The apiserver cannot serve without its datastore.

trbl.q: Which command shows why a pod was evicted?
o: kubectl get events is enough alone
trbl.w: describe shows the reason and the node conditions.

trbl.q: A Service has endpoints but connections time out. Next check?
o: The NetworkPolicy and the container port
trbl.w: Endpoints exist, so the problem is policy or port level.

trbl.q: kubelet is not running on a node. Node status?
trbl.w: Without kubelet heartbeats the node controller marks it NotReady.

trbl.q: Which logs show the previous crashed container output?
trbl.w: --previous reads the last terminated instance.

trbl.q: kubectl logs fails but the container runs. Where else can you look?
trbl.w: The kubelet writes container logs under /var/log/pods.

trbl.q: An empty /etc/cni/net.d explains:
trbl.w: No CNI config means no pod network.

trbl.q: Which command lists containers on a node when the apiserver is down?
trbl.w: crictl talks to the runtime socket directly.

trbl.q: A task resists for five minutes. Best move?
o: Flag it and move to the next task
trbl.w: Passing candidates all report the same strategy: come back later.

items.c:
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
etcdctl snapshot restore /backup/etcd.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore

kubeadm certs check-expiration
kubeadm certs renew all

kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods
kubectl create rolebinding rb --role=pod-reader --user=jane -n dev
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=jane -n dev

kubeadm upgrade plan
kubeadm upgrade apply v1.30.0
kubectl drain node1 --ignore-daemonsets
kubeadm upgrade node

ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests
# kubelet runs everything in that directory

kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=3
kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:1.27
kubectl rollout status deployment/web
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web --to-revision=1

kubectl create configmap app --from-literal=COLOR=blue
kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=password=s3cr3t

nodeSelector:
  disk: ssd
# or
tolerations:
- key: dedicated
  operator: Equal
  value: gpu
  effect: NoSchedule

livenessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 10
kubectl expose deployment web --port=80 --target-port=8080 --type=NodePort

kubectl get endpoints web
kubectl get svc web -o wide

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {role: db}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector: {matchLabels: {role: frontend}}
kubectl run tmp --image=busybox --rm -it -- nslookup kubernetes.default
kubectl create ingress web --rule="host/path=svc:80"

kubectl create -f pvc.yaml
kubectl get pvc
kubectl describe pvc data

kubectl get storageclass
kubectl patch storageclass standard -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class":"true"}}}'

kubectl get pods -A -o wide
kubectl describe pod <pod>
kubectl logs <pod> --previous
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

systemctl status kubelet
journalctl -u kubelet -n 50 --no-pager
kubectl describe node <node>

kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh
kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container>

kubectl get svc,endpoints
kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80

kubectl rollout restart deployment/web
kubectl delete pod <pod> --force --grace-period=0

tips.p: CKA questions are short but dense. Note the namespace, the object name and the exact change requested before typing anything.
kubectl create and kubectl run save minutes. Use --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate a manifest, then edit it.
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=dev. Every later command then targets the right namespace.
export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml", then kubectl run nginx --image=nginx $do > pod.yaml.
Memorise the three certificate flags. The exam gives you the endpoints but not the flags.
kubectl drain node1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data, and uncordon afterwards.
A pod that never starts has no logs. describe shows the scheduler and kubelet events.
Empty endpoints mean a label selector mismatch. Fix the selector, not the Service.
Policies are enforced only if the CNI supports them. A policy that seems ignored is often a CNI limitation.
Before deleting a PVC in the exam, check the StorageClass reclaim policy. Delete may destroy the data.
First pass: solve the easy questions. Flag the heavy ones and come back. Every question is worth the same.
Run kubectl get on what you created. An object that exists but does not work scores zero.

tips.t: Book only when mocks are above 80%
tips.p: People who pass report the same pattern: two or three full mock exams above 80% before booking. Below that, the time pressure wins.
Two minutes at the start: alias k=kubectl, export do='--dry-run=client -o yaml', and set vi to show line numbers. You will type hundreds of commands.
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.livenessProbe gives the exact field names offline. Faster than guessing YAML.
The exam UI lets you copy from the question. Copy namespace, object name and context instead of retyping them; typos cost points.
Twenty tasks in 120 minutes leaves no room for perfectionism. If a task resists for more than six minutes, flag it and move on.
One third of the score. Practise breaking a cluster on purpose: stop kubelet, corrupt a Service selector, fill a disk.

tips.t: Practise on kubeadm, not only kind
tips.p: Static pods, certificates and etcd only make sense on a kubeadm cluster. The exam tests those directly.

tips.t: Read the last line of the task first
tips.p: Tasks often end with the exact verification: a pod Running, a PVC Bound, a curl returning a specific string. Solve towards that check.

tips.t: Do not fix what is not asked
tips.p: If a task asks for one thing, do not repair the rest of the cluster. Extra changes can break other tasks that share the cluster.
kubectl get, describe, or curl. A created object that does not work is worth zero, and partial credit only comes from a working part.

tips.t: Documentation is a skill, not a safety net
tips.p: One candidate spent weeks memorising YAML, then realised the real skill is finding the right docs page in 30 seconds. Pre-open kubectl cheat sheet, NetworkPolicy, PV, probes and RBAC.
Reports converge: first killer.sh run often lands under 30%, then above 70% after two weeks of hands-on. Book only when you finish the mock inside the two hours, not after.
Identity verification takes time. Candidates who joined late started stressed and lost minutes they never recovered.
The real CKA is 100% hands-on tasks. If a resource claims MCQs, it is a different exam or an old format.

tips.t: Adapt manifests instead of writing them
tips.p: kubectl get deploy web -o yaml > web.yaml, edit two lines, apply. This single habit saves ten minutes per exam.
/etc/kubernetes/manifests, /var/lib/kubelet, /var/lib/kubelet/pki, /var/log/pods, /etc/cni/net.d, /etc/kubernetes/pki. Half the troubleshooting tasks are decided there.

body.p: Online, proctored, performance-based. Two hours to solve around 15 to 20 tasks on real clusters, in a browser terminal. No multiple choice on the real exam: everything is hands-on.
Several clusters, each task tells you which context to use. You may open kubernetes.io/docs, kubernetes.io/blog and helm.sh/docs in a second tab. Nothing else.
Each task is weighted. Partial credit exists for multi-step tasks, so always do the easy part even if you cannot finish. The published passing score is 66%.
The certification lasts two years, includes one retake, and the exam eligibility window is 12 months from purchase.
The exam currently runs Kubernetes v1.37. Check the official page before booking, the version moves.
Almost guaranteed. Learn the three certificate flags by heart, and remember that restore needs the static pod hostPath updated and etcd restarted.
Create a Role or ClusterRole, bind it, verify with kubectl auth can-i --as. Know the difference between Role and ClusterRole for cluster-scoped resources.
Upgrade a control plane node, add a worker. Drain, upgrade kubeadm, kubeadm upgrade node, uncordon.
Forgetting to switch context or namespace before applying. The object is created, just in the wrong place, which scores zero.
set image, rollout status, rollout undo --to-revision. Know that rollout history only shows revisions if change-cause is annotated.
Create ConfigMaps and Secrets both from literals and from files, then consume them as envFrom and as volumes. Remember volumes refresh, env vars do not.
nodeSelector for the simple case, nodeAffinity for required and preferred, taints and tolerations for repulsion. Combine them in one task and check the pod lands where asked.
Set requests and limits, then explain QoS. A BestEffort pod is evicted first, which is often the hidden question.
Know the three types and the port trio: port, targetPort, nodePort. Most failures are a targetPort that does not match the container.
kubectl get endpoints tells you instantly whether the selector matches. Empty endpoints is a labelling bug, not a network bug.
Policies are additive and only apply to selected pods. Write a default deny, then allow one source, and test from a temporary pod.
service.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Test with a busybox pod; if DNS fails, look at CoreDNS in kube-system.

docs.t: Storage: the short chapter, the easy points

body.p: Write a PV by hand once: capacity, accessModes, hostPath. Then a PVC that binds to it. Check the STATUS column.
Dynamic provisioning means no PV manifest. Know the default class annotation and the reclaim policies.
volumeClaimTemplates creates one PVC per replica. That is the only way to give each pod its own disk.
WaitForFirstConsumer leaves the PVC Pending until a pod uses it. Do not panic, and do not delete it.
get, describe, logs, events, exec. Always in that order. describe gives the scheduler and kubelet reasons, logs give the application.
Pending is scheduling, ImagePullBackOff is the image or the pull secret, CrashLoopBackOff is the app or a bad liveness probe.
systemctl status kubelet, journalctl -u kubelet, crictl ps -a. A stopped kubelet means NotReady within a minute.
Empty endpoints, wrong targetPort, NetworkPolicy, DNS. Four checks cover almost every case.

docs.t: How to prepare, from people who passed

body.p: Every report says the same thing: watching does not work. Build a cluster, break it, fix it. kubeadm in a VM or kind locally is enough.
kubectl run, create deployment, create service, expose, with --dry-run=client -o yaml. Then edit the YAML. Typing full manifests from scratch is what makes people run out of time.
First pass: everything you can solve in under five minutes. Flag the rest. Come back with 40 minutes left.
After each task, run kubectl get on the object and check it is Running, Bound or has endpoints. A created object that does not work earns nothing.
Prepare the doc pages you will need: kubectl cheat sheet, NetworkPolicy, PV, probes, taints. You cannot browse freely, but you can pre-open tabs.
Join the proctoring session early. Identity check, room scan, then the exam environment opens. Late joiners lose minutes they never get back.
Set aliases (k=kubectl, export do='--dry-run=client -o yaml'), open the docs tab, and write your six paths on paper if scratch paper is allowed.
Solve everything you recognise instantly. Flag anything that resists more than five minutes. Aim to have 12 of 20 tasks done.
Attack the flagged ones. Adapt existing YAML rather than writing from scratch. Verify with kubectl get after each.
Re-verify every created object: Running, Bound, endpoints, curl. Fix only what is cheap to fix. Do not start a new complex task.

docs.t: Finding answers in the docs fast

body.p: kubectl cheat sheet, NetworkPolicy, PersistentVolume, liveness/readiness probes, taints and tolerations, RBAC.
Every one of those pages contains a complete manifest. Copy it, change the names, apply. That is the intended workflow.
Ctrl+F on the page beats the site search. Search for the API field name, not for the concept.
kubernetes.io/docs, kubernetes.io/blog, helm.sh/docs. Nothing else, and no AI assistant.
etcd snapshot and restore; create a Role and bind it; kubeadm upgrade a control plane; add a worker; renew certificates; inspect static pod manifests.
Rolling update and rollback; ConfigMap as env and as volume; Secret as file; resource requests and limits; nodeSelector and affinity; taint and toleration; Job and CronJob; init container.
ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer; fix empty endpoints; NetworkPolicy default deny plus allow; Ingress with TLS; test DNS from a pod.
Create a PV and a PVC that binds; StorageClass default; StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates; mount a ConfigMap.
Pod Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff; node NotReady; Service without endpoints; kubelet logs; CoreDNS failure; expired certificate.

labs.brief: Take a consistent snapshot of etcd on the control plane node, then verify it.
labs.sol:
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd.db --write-out=table
labs.check: The status output shows a revision and a non-zero key count.

labs.brief: User jane must list and get pods in namespace dev, nothing more.
labs.sol:
kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods -n dev
kubectl create rolebinding jane-read --role=pod-reader --user=jane -n dev
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=jane -n dev
labs.check: can-i answers yes for list, no for delete.

labs.brief: Upgrade a worker node to the next available kubeadm version and bring it back.
labs.sol:
kubectl drain node1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.30.0-1.1
kubeadm upgrade node
apt-get install -y kubelet=1.30.0-1.1 kubectl=1.30.0-1.1
systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl uncordon node1
labs.check: kubectl get nodes shows the new version and Ready.

labs.brief: Set the current context namespace to dev and prove it.
labs.sol:
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=dev
kubectl config view --minify | grep namespace
labs.check: The minified config shows namespace: dev.

labs.brief: Update the image of deployment web to nginx:1.27, watch the rollout, then roll back.
labs.sol:
kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:1.27
kubectl rollout status deployment/web
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web
kubectl rollout status deployment/web
labs.check: After undo, the pods run the previous image.

labs.brief: Create a ConfigMap from a file and mount it in a pod, plus expose one key as an env var.
labs.sol:
kubectl create configmap app --from-file=app.conf
kubectl run cfg --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > p.yaml
# add volumeMounts + volumes, and env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef
kubectl apply -f p.yaml
labs.check: kubectl exec cfg -- cat /etc/app/app.conf prints the file.

labs.brief: Create a pod with requests and limits that gets the Guaranteed QoS class.
labs.sol:
# requests == limits for cpu and memory on every container
kubectl run g --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > g.yaml
# set requests=limits
kubectl apply -f g.yaml
kubectl get pod g -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
labs.check: The qosClass is Guaranteed.

labs.brief: Taint node1 with dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule, then run a pod that tolerates it.
labs.sol:
kubectl taint nodes node1 dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule
# add tolerations to the pod spec
kubectl run gpu --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > g.yaml
kubectl apply -f g.yaml
labs.check: kubectl get pod -o wide shows node1.

labs.brief: Create a Job with 3 completions and a CronJob running every 5 minutes.
labs.sol:
kubectl create job once --image=busybox -- echo done
kubectl create cronjob every5 --image=busybox --schedule='*/5 * * * *' -- echo tick
labs.check: kubectl get job shows COMPLETIONS 1/1, get cronjob shows the schedule.

labs.brief: Expose deployment web on port 80 targeting container port 8080, as NodePort.
labs.sol:
kubectl expose deployment web --port=80 --target-port=8080 --type=NodePort
kubectl get svc web -o wide
labs.check: Endpoints are populated and the NodePort is in 30000-32767.

labs.brief: A Service returns nothing. Find why and fix it without touching the Service spec.
labs.sol:
kubectl get endpoints web
kubectl get pods --show-labels
# label the pods to match the Service selector
kubectl label pod <pod> app=web
labs.check: kubectl get endpoints web now lists pod IPs.

labs.brief: Deny all ingress in namespace dev, then allow only pods labelled role=frontend to reach role=db on 5432.
labs.sol:
# policy 1: podSelector {} policyTypes [Ingress]
# policy 2: podSelector role=db, ingress from podSelector role=frontend, ports 5432
kubectl apply -f netpol.yaml
labs.check: kubectl describe netpol shows both selectors.

labs.brief: From a temporary pod, resolve a Service by short name and by FQDN.
labs.sol:
kubectl run tmp --image=busybox --rm -it -- sh
nslookup web
nslookup web.dev.svc.cluster.local
labs.check: Both return an IP, the FQDN one always.

labs.brief: Create a TLS secret and route host demo.local to service web on port 80.
labs.sol:
kubectl create secret tls demo-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key
kubectl create ingress demo --rule='demo.local/=web:80' --tls=demo.local=demo-tls
labs.check: kubectl describe ingress demo shows the rule and the TLS section.

labs.t: Bind a PVC to a PV
labs.brief: Create a 1Gi hostPath PV with ReadWriteOnce, and a PVC that binds to it.
labs.sol:
# pv.yaml: capacity 1Gi, accessModes [ReadWriteOnce], hostPath /mnt/data
kubectl apply -f pv.yaml
# pvc.yaml: requests storage 1Gi, same access mode
kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml
kubectl get pvc
labs.check: STATUS is Bound, and the PV shows Claim: default/<name>.

labs.brief: Mark an existing StorageClass as the cluster default.
labs.sol: kubectl patch storageclass standard -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class":"true"}}}'
labs.check: kubectl get sc shows (default) next to the class.

labs.brief: Create a StatefulSet of 2 replicas with a volumeClaimTemplate of 1Gi.
labs.sol:
# volumeClaimTemplates: name data, 1Gi, ReadWriteOnce
kubectl apply -f sts.yaml
kubectl get pvc
labs.check: Two PVCs named data-<statefulset>-0 and -1, both Bound.

labs.brief: A pod never schedules. Find the reason and make it run.
labs.sol:
kubectl describe pod <pod>
# read Events: insufficient cpu, or nodeSelector, or taint
kubectl get nodes --show-labels
# fix the selector or lower the requests
labs.check: kubectl get pod shows Running on the expected node.

labs.brief: A container restarts in a loop. Find the cause from the logs and fix the manifest.
labs.sol:
kubectl logs <pod> --previous
kubectl describe pod <pod>
# often a bad livenessProbe or a wrong command
labs.check: The pod is Running with 0 restarts after a minute.

labs.brief: A pod cannot pull its image. Identify whether it is the name, the tag or a pull secret.
labs.sol:
kubectl describe pod <pod>
# check the exact image string and the Events
# if private: kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred ...
# add imagePullSecrets to the pod spec
labs.check: The pod reaches Running.

labs.brief: A worker is NotReady. Find the cause on the node and restore it.
labs.sol:
kubectl describe node <node>
ssh <node>
systemctl status kubelet
journalctl -u kubelet -n 50 --no-pager
systemctl restart kubelet
labs.check: kubectl get nodes shows Ready within a minute.

labs.brief: A Service answers nothing from another pod. Find the broken link.
labs.sol:
kubectl get endpoints <svc>
kubectl get svc <svc> -o yaml | grep -E 'port|targetPort'
kubectl exec tmp -- wget -qO- http://<svc>:80
labs.check: curl or wget returns the app response.

labs.brief: List the control plane certificates and their expiry dates.
labs.sol: kubeadm certs check-expiration
labs.check: Every certificate shows a date in the future.
